interview.interviewer_instructions: You are a McKinsey case interviewer conducting a spoken mock interview. Ask ONE question at a time and wait for the candidate's spoken answer before continuing. The 'expected_answer', 'red_flags', and 'followups' fields are YOUR PRIVATE KEY — never read them aloud or reveal them. Only reveal a 'clarifying_data' value if the candidate explicitly asks for it. After each answer, silently judge it as strong / vague / wrong and ask the matching follow-up. Stay professionally neutral. Move to the next question once the current one is resolved. Keep your spoken turns short.

questions.question: Our client is a mid-size grocery retailer in the UAE. Over the last two years their profit has fallen roughly 30% even though revenue is flat. How would you structure your approach to finding out why?

key_points: Profit = Revenue − Cost; revenue is flat, so isolate the cost side first
Breaks revenue into price × volume, cost into fixed vs variable, MECE
States a hypothesis to test before diving in
expected_answer.sample_strong_answer: Since revenue is flat but profit fell, the driver is likely on the cost side or a mix shift. I'd decompose profit into revenue (price × volume, by category) and cost (COGS, labour, rent, logistics), then find which line moved most.
red_flags: Jumps to solutions with no structure
Ignores that revenue is flat and chases revenue growth

followups.if_strong: Good structure. Where would you look first, and why?
followups.if_vague: Can you make that MECE? What are the top-level buckets of profit?
followups.if_wrong: Revenue is flat — does chasing more sales fit the problem we described?

questions.question: You said to look at costs. What kinds of costs would you expect a grocery retailer to have, and which would you investigate first?

key_points: COGS (product purchase cost) is the largest line for grocery
Then labour, rent/occupancy, logistics/cold chain, wastage/spoilage
Prioritises by size and by what plausibly changed over two years
expected_answer.sample_strong_answer: COGS dominates grocery margins, so I'd start there, then labour and rent. Given two years of change, I'd check supplier cost inflation and spoilage before fixed costs like rent.
red_flags: Starts with the smallest cost lines

followups.if_strong: Let's get some numbers on that.
followups.if_vague: Of those, which is usually the biggest for a grocer?
followups.if_wrong: Would rent typically swing profit 30% in two years?

questions.question: Here's the data. Revenue is 500 million AED per year, unchanged. Two years ago gross margin was 22%; today it's 16%. Fixed costs (rent, admin) are 70 million AED and haven't changed. What has happened to operating profit, in numbers?

key_points: Profit fell from 40M to 10M — a 75% drop, driven entirely by margin
expected_answer.sample_strong_answer: Gross profit went from 110 million to 80 million, a 30 million drop. With fixed costs flat at 70 million, operating profit fell from 40 million to 10 million — down 75%. The entire decline is the gross margin dropping from 22% to 16%.
red_flags: Doesn't connect it back to the margin driver

followups.if_strong: Right — 40 down to 10. So what's driving the margin from 22% to 16%?
followups.if_vague: Start with gross profit: what's 22% of 500 million?
followups.if_wrong: Check that step — gross profit is margin times revenue. Try again.

questions.question: The 6-point margin drop is the whole story. What could cause gross margin to fall from 22% to 16% while prices to customers stayed the same?

key_points: Supplier/purchase cost inflation not passed to shelf prices
Higher spoilage/wastage (fresh categories) raising effective COGS
Shrinkage/theft or discounting/promotions eroding realised price
expected_answer.sample_strong_answer: If shelf prices held but margin fell, purchase costs rose without a price pass-through — supplier inflation. I'd also check spoilage in fresh goods and a mix shift toward low-margin staples.
red_flags: Blames revenue/volume when we established prices held
Only names one cause with no way to test it

followups.if_strong: Good hypotheses. How would you confirm which one it is?
followups.if_vague: Prices held but cost of goods rose — what does that point to?
followups.if_wrong: We said prices to customers were unchanged — so is this a revenue problem?

questions.question: Assume it's mostly supplier cost inflation the client absorbed. Give me your recommendation to the CEO.

key_points: Clear stance: restore margin via price pass-through and/or cost action
Concrete levers: renegotiate supplier terms, selective price increases on inelastic items, own-brand substitution, cut spoilage
Quantifies the goal (recover ~6 margin points ≈ 30M gross profit)
Names a risk (price increases hurting volume) and a next step
expected_answer.sample_strong_answer: I'd recommend recovering the 6 margin points worth ~30 million: renegotiate supplier contracts, pass through selective price rises on price-inelastic staples, and push higher-margin own brands. Risk is volume loss from price rises, so test on a few categories first. Next step: a category-level margin bridge to size each lever.
red_flags: Recommends generic cost-cutting unrelated to the margin cause

followups.if_strong: Strong close. What's the single biggest risk to that plan?
followups.if_vague: What's your one-line recommendation, and how much profit does it recover?
followups.if_wrong: Does that address the margin cause we identified?
